name: Log cabins at Wolf Point

documented_range.note: ONE SOURCE, ONE YEAR, AND THE LONGEST UNSUPPORTED RUN IN THIS DATASET. Wau-Bun, describing 1831: 'Near him [Wentworth's tavern] were two or three log cabins occupied by Robinson, the Pottowattamie chief, and some of his wife's connexions.' That is the whole of the evidence, and it is a single sentence in a book written twenty-five years after the year it describes. Nothing reached follows these cabins to 1832 or to any year after. The range is closed at the end of 1835 on the ordinary continuity argument — a standing building stands until something says otherwise — and that argument is under more strain here than anywhere else in the dataset, because THE FOUR YEARS THIS RANGE CROSSES ARE THE YEARS OF THE REMOVAL. The 1833 Treaty of Chicago ceded the land; through 1835 the Potawatomi were assembled around the town awaiting removal west; Billy Caldwell, who Wau-Bun says resided at Wolf Point occasionally, led his people west in 1835; and Alexander Robinson held a reserve of his own on the Des Plaines from the 1829 treaty and lived out his life there. A house left by the people who built it is a house that comes down or is taken over, and no source records either happening to these. WHAT THIS RECORD CLAIMS IS THAT THE BUILDINGS STOOD, NOT THAT ANYONE WAS IN THEM. If evidence turns up that they were gone by July 1835 this record leaves the scene for data/exclusions.json, and that is a likelier outcome for this record than for any other in the parcel.

change_note: The log cabins standing in the west-bank row at Wolf Point in 1831, between Wentworth's tavern and the log meeting house north of it. This record models the buildings only; it makes no claim about who was in them on the scene date.

placement.position_note: A POINT CHOSEN IN A ROW, NOT A DERIVATION, so it is tagged conjectural and cites no sources. What Wau-Bun gives is an ORDER along the west bank and no distances: 'Facing down the river from the west was, first a small tavern kept by Mr. Wentworth ... Near him were two or three log cabins occupied by Robinson ... A little remote from these residences was a small square log building, originally designed for a school-house.' So the cabins lie between this project's wolf_point_tavern (north face at local N -45) and its walker_meeting_house (south face at local N -10), and 'a little remote' says the meeting house stands clear of them. This coordinate splits that gap, about 20 m north of the tavern and 14 m south of the meeting house, and sets the cabin back from the water on the same frontage. THE UNCERTAINTY IS THE ROW'S, NOT A METRE FIGURE: both neighbours are themselves placed from bank geometry rather than from any surviving intersection — the Walker meeting house's own position is tagged conjectural and may be on the wrong bank entirely — so this record inherits two soft positions and adds a free choice between them. Treat it as good to about ±40 m along the bank and no better. Facade bearing 90, due east onto the river, follows Wau-Bun's 'facing down the river from the west' and the bearing this project gives the tavern and the meeting house in the same row.
placement.symbolic_location: West bank at Wolf Point, near Wentworth's tavern (the Wolf Point Tavern), in the river-front row between the tavern and the log meeting house to the north.

footprint.note: PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED. 6.5 x 5 m is about 21 x 16 ft, an ordinary single-pen log cabin of the type and period. Every number is invented. AND THE POLYGON IS ONE CABIN WHERE THE SOURCE COUNTS TWO OR THREE: see form.cabin_count, which records the number and declares that the model does not build it.

construction.note: 'two or three log cabins' — Wau-Bun. The fabric is the one physical fact the source gives.

cabin_count.note: Wau-Bun counts them loosely — 'two or three' — and the looseness is the evidence, so the value is kept as the source's words rather than resolved to a number. ONE CABIN IS BUILT. The archetype models a building, not a group, and choosing two or three would mean inventing the count the source declined to give, plus their spacing and their arrangement. So the model understates the place: a visitor sees one cabin where there were at least two, and the record says so here.

stories.note: Not attested. A single-pen log cabin is single-storey by type, and everything else in this row is described as low.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 2.4 m is about 8 ft, a single-pen log wall — the same reading this project gives the Sauganash's 1829 cabin.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for log construction of this type, period and region.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 35 degrees is the archetype's mid-range for a low log cabin roofed in riven shakes. Inferred from construction practice, not measured.

chimneys.note: Not attested. One is the normal number for a single-pen log cabin lived in through Chicago winters. The COUNT is the inference; position, size and material are the archetype's — docs/LIBERTIES.md L26.

function.note: Wau-Bun calls them cabins 'occupied by' named people and later refers to the group as 'these residences'. They were homes.

residents.name: The Robinson household at Wolf Point
residents.why: Wau-Bun, describing 1831: 'Near him [Wentworth's tavern] were two or three log cabins occupied by Robinson, the Pottowattamie chief, and some of his wife's connexions.' data/structures/robinson_caldwell_cabins.json exists on that single sentence and carries review_required: true for the same reason this household does. Andreas independently puts him at Wolf Point with a store or trading-house in the later part of his residence.

persons.name: Alexander Robinson (Che-che-pin-qua)
persons.note: A CHIEF, A LICENSED TRADER AND A RECORDED VOTER OF THE SETTLEMENT. Andreas: born at Mackinaw about 1762, his father a Scots trader who had been an officer in the British army and his mother an Ottawa woman; he sheltered the Kinzie family after the 1812 massacre and carried Captain and Mrs Heald three hundred miles by bark canoe to Mackinaw. His personal property was assessed at $200 by the Peoria County assessor in 1825 and he is recorded as a voter in 1825, 1826 and 1830. He married Catherine Chevalier, daughter of the chief Francois Chevalier, on 28 September 1826, John Kinzie officiating as justice of the peace, and became chief of her father's band at his death. By the treaty of Prairie du Chien of July 1829 he was granted two sections on the Des Plaines; by Camp Tippecanoe in 1832 a life annuity of $200; and by the Chicago treaty of September 1833 a further $300 a year for life.

persons.name: Catherine Chevalier Robinson
persons.note: NAMED, WITH A MARRIAGE DATE, A FATHER AND A DEATH DATE - which makes her one of only four women in this parcel documented in her own right rather than as 'Mrs'. Andreas: married 28 September 1826 by John Kinzie, J.P.; daughter of Francois and Mary Ann Chevalier, her father chief of a united band of Potawatomi, Ottawa and Chippewa with his village at the Calumet; she died 7 August 1860 and is buried with her husband on the bank of the Des Plaines.

persons.name: The rest of the Robinson household, unnamed
persons.note: AN ADMISSION, NOT A PERSON. Wau-Bun describes 'two or three log cabins occupied by Robinson, the Pottowattamie chief, and some of his wife's connexions' - so the household extended beyond the couple and the source neither names nor counts it. Andreas has him settling on the Des Plaines reservation 'with his family' after the removal, and two sons and a daughter-in-law buried beside him. Do not count this entry as a person.

residents.research_note: A DOCUMENTED HOUSEHOLD OF THREE NAMED OR COUNTED PEOPLE WHO WERE LIVING AT WOLF POINT WHEN THE TOWN GREW UP AROUND THEM. STANDING CONSTRAINT. AGENTS.md: the final removal of the Potawatomi from Chicago occurred in August 1835, inside this project's first target year and six weeks AFTER the scene date; Native presence, representation and depiction are not research gaps to be filled by inference, and v1 ships no human figures at all. This record is a dataset entry that states what named sources say about a named person and adds nothing. It carries review_required so that no scene containing it can be marked released before the consultation the project has committed to. TWO DATING PROBLEMS ARE RECORDED AND NOT RESOLVED. First, Andreas dates the last great assembly and the departure for the Missouri to 1836 under Captain Russell and Billy Caldwell, while this project's own source chicagology_lastwardance places the last war dance at Chicago on 18 August 1835; the two readings differ by a year and both are AFTER 1 July 1835, so the scene date is unaffected and the disagreement is recorded rather than averaged. Second, Wau-Bun describes 1831 and this scene is 1835; the structure record already says its four-year run is 'the longest unsupported run in this dataset' and that the years it crosses are the years of the removal. This household claims that the people were there, on the same evidence and with the same warning.

citations.citation: Andreas, A. T. History of Chicago: From the Earliest Period to the Present Time. Vol. 1. Chicago: A. T. Andreas, 1884.
Kinzie, Juliette A. M. Wau-Bun: The 'Early Day' in the North-West. New York: Derby & Jackson, 1856.

research_note: THE HARDEST RECORD IN THIS PARCEL TO GET RIGHT, AND IT IS FLAGGED review_required: Wau-Bun attests these cabins in 1831 as the home of Alexander Robinson, the Potawatomi chief, and members of his wife’s family, and 1835 is the year of the final removal of the Potawatomi from Chicago. Wau-Bun's single sentence of 1831 attests two or three log cabins near Wentworth's tavern occupied by Alexander Robinson, the Potawatomi chief, and members of his wife's family, with Billy Caldwell residing there occasionally. FOUR THINGS ARE UNATTESTED AT THE SCENE DATE and each is recorded where it belongs rather than resolved: whether the cabins still stood in July 1835 (documented_range), how many there were and how they sat (form.cabin_count and the footprint), exactly where in the row they were (position), and who if anyone was in them — which is why this record carries no occupants block at all. THE TENSION THAT MATTERS is the last one crossed with the date: 1835 is the year of the final removal of the Potawatomi from Chicago, the most historically significant event of this project's first target year. AGENTS.md is explicit that Native presence is not a research gap to be filled by inference and that depiction requires consultation. So this record builds the BUILT ENVIRONMENT — a log cabin on a bank — and asserts nothing about people, and the review_required flag holds the scene short of release until someone qualified has looked at it. WHAT WOULD UPGRADE IT: any source that follows these cabins past 1831 — the 1833 treaty's schedules of improvements and claims, the agency's correspondence, or the Chicago Democrat. See docs/RESEARCH/robinson_caldwell_cabins.md.
